subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has already indicated that Bill C-193 deals with individual tax cuts, as announced by the minister in his recent budget, by increasing income tax exemptions and by initiating for the first time a 5 per cent tax cut on a progressive basis with a minimum of $100 and a maximum of $500. This is to be effective next year. There is also provision for indexing taxes about which I will comment later.
That part of the measure now before us is wholeheartedly welcomed by members of this party. I refer to the $100 tax cut based on a progressive formula. The tax cut of $100 as a minimum will mean quite a bit more to those in low income groups. The minister has given us one or two examples of this fact in his remarks today. The ceiling of $500 is a good step in our taxation system. I think this system, once initiated by parliament, should be seen as an example for the future when we are talking about tax reform in this country. Because of this, the NDP will support the bill before us and will not hold it up in any way.
I think this party deserves some of the credit for this progresive step. Hon. members will recall that back in November and December when we were talking about making this parliament work, one of the things we wanted was tax reform in a way which would allow the low and middle income people to receive a bit of a tax break from the federal government. This is one of the measures members of this party welcome; we are happy it is now being presented to the House and will soon be law. This should be the vanguard of a complete reform of the taxation system in Canada. 1 think we still have a very unfair taxation system which places a heavier tax burden on low and middle income earners than on the wealthy and privileged people in our society. Our system allows the wealthy and privileged to take advantage of many tax loopholes so as not to pay their fair share. I should like to give one or two examples of what I mean.
In many cases, the lower and middle income taxpayer pays a higher percentage of his income in taxation than some people in the higher tax brackets. The bill before us today will correct this situation to some extent. I think this is only a small step in the right direction and for that reason I think it only right to put some of our viewpoints on record at this time. For example, let us take some figures from the Federation of Labour In Ontario, some 1970 statistics about a family of four and the amount of income they pay in taxes. This is both hidden and direct taxes, both federal and provincial; in other words, all the taxes that a family of four in the province of Ontario
June 18, 1973

would pay. I will give two or three examples of families with different amounts of income.
First of all, there is the family with an annual income of $5,200. In 1970 they paid 37.8 per cent of their income in taxation, that is, federal and provincial taxes as well as hidden taxes such as in food and gasoline, across the board. A family of four in Ontario with an income of $10,400 paid 37.6 per cent of their income in taxes. In other words, they paid a slightly smaller percentage of their income in taxes despite the fact that they had twice as much income, at $10,400, compared with $5,200.1 think that is one very good indication of an example where a family with a smaller income pays a greater percentage of their total income in taxes than a family with a higher income.
Another example I have here is a chart taken from the report on poverty by the Senate last year or the year before. It is based on Statistics Canada figures. Unfortunately, these figures are about 12 years old, but I am told that they are the most recent on the percentage of income that certain families pay in taxes. Again, this is total taxation both direct and indirect. According to these statistics, people earning under $2,000 a year in 1961 paid some 60 per cent of their income in taxation. If they went up from $2,000 to $3,000 a year, they paid 32.9 per cent of their income in taxes. If they earned between $3,000 and $4,000, they paid 32.2 per cent of their income in taxes. If they earned between $5,000 and $6,000, they paid 32.8 per cent of their income in taxes. Those with $10,000 a year and up paid 38.4 per cent of their income in taxes.
I think that some of these basic statistics from Statistics Canada, from the Senate report on poverty and from the Ontario Federation of Labour indicate the reasons why we should be more progressive in the taxation laws of this country, and I commend the government for the one step forward they have made today of the $100 tax cut as the minimum. I think that is progressive and that is the way we should go when we talk about reform of the taxation system across the board, because taxes, as I have already indicated, often hit the working classes hardest. They hit the low income person much more than the middle or high income person. For example, everybody, regardless of income, has to buy bread. The Economic Council of Canada says that in a loaf of bread you may have as many as 150 indirect or hidden taxes. You can see here that when you have hidden taxes of this sort there is bound to be a regressive taxation system that will hit the lower income person harder than the one with a higher income. That is the type of system we must try to change as rapidly as possible.
The second point I want to make tonight-and I will ask a few questions on this when we reach committee of the whole stage-concerns the new system that the minister has introduced, of indexing our income tax system. As I understand it, it will be the type of system according to which if a person pays 20 per cent of his income in taxes this year, his taxes next year, taking inflation into consideration, will be adjusted or indexed so that 20 per cent of his income next year will also be paid in taxes. One of the things that worries me, if my interpretation of the indexing system is correct, is that the system may not be very progressive; that a person who is earning a higher income
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
will be gaining more from that type of system. I think it works that way because it follows the general idea or rule which our tax exemption system follows now. When there is a tax exemption of, say, $100 or $200 for everyone across the board, it is the person earning the higher income who benefits most.
I will give the House a couple of examples of what I mean by the tax exemption system, under our law, assisting most the higher income people. Our party says that instead of an exemption system we should have a tax credit system which would help the lower income people to a greater degree than do exemptions. I have here figures that I have worked out based on last year's legislation when exemptions for a single person went up to $1,500. One can see here how the increase of $500 has assisted, in this taxation year, those with a higher income more than those who have less.
Take, for example, a person with a gross income of $2,000. If he was a single person with no dependants and had a $1,000 exemption, he was paying $109 in taxes. Last year, when that exemption was increased to $1,500, his tax bill went down to $75. In other words, this person saved some $33 because the tax exemption was increased from $1,000 to $1,500. consider a person with no dependants earnings $4,000 a year and taking advantage of the same tax exemption. His tax bill went down from $707 to $547, a net saving of $160. A person earning $8,000 a year saves $195; a person earning $25,000 a year saves, because of the increased exemption, $297. You can see the inequity in this type of system.
I suggest that instead of a tax exemption system, we should have in this country a tax credit system which would help the low income people more. We have an example of that in the bill before us, in the clause that provides for a 5 per cent income tax cut across the board, with a guaranteed minimum of a $100 tax cut for every citizen regardless of income and a maximum tax cut of $500. That is the type of system we should adopt in Canada; It would be much more equitable.
The third point that I want to make in this debate is that we should be striving as hard as possible to make our taxation laws more progressive in terms of what the ordinary people pay compared with the wealthy people or compared with some of the corporations in this country. If you look at the statistics, you find that the amount of revenue the federal and provincial governments have collected over the past 10 or 12 years from individuals, compared with those collected from corporations, indicates a developing trend which I and my party do not like at all.
I have here some figures from Statistics Canada which indicate that governments, both federal and provincial, are collecting less and less of their taxes from corporations as compared with individuals. To the federal income tax in 1962. 11 years ago, corporations contributed 38 per cent while individuals contributed 62 per cent. In 1970, corporations contributed 26 per cent, and individuals 74 per cent. You can see the tremendous increase in the tax burden on individuals as compared with the corporate sector. These, I may remind the House, are figures compiled before the corporate tax bill which we were debating previously was brought forward.

June 18, 1973
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
The same thing is true of the taxes collected by our provincial governments. It is true to an even more startling degree than the taxes collected by the federal government. In 1962, for example, 57 per cent of the taxes collected by provincial governments came from corporations, and 43 per cent from individuals. By 1970, only 22 per cent of the taxes collected by provincial governments came from corporations, and 78 per cent came from individuals. This is a trend that must be stopped, that must be reversed in terms of our economy in general, in terms of producing jobs and wealth and in terms of a more equalized taxation system where people pay taxes on their ability to pay, and where income will be taxed no matter where it is derived, whether from work in a factory, from clipping coupons or, indeed, from capital gains.
The taxation system in this country, as has been pointed out by our party and by Eric Kierans, both when he was a member of this House and after leaving it, has a very unfair and discriminating feature when it comes to dealing with industries. The gas and oil companies, as the House well knows, over the past ten years have paid taxes on only 5 per cent to 7 per cent of their book profits, and the mining companies have paid taxes on only 13 per cent of their book profits. A waitress in a cafe, a single person with no dependants, earning the minimum wage, is probably paying a higher rate of tax than the gas and oil companies. Why am I so concerned about that? I am concerned because we have a very unfair taxation system. But even greater than that, when you give that type of incentive to the extractive industries-and they are the capital-intensive industries-very few jobs are created.
Canada has a very high unemployment rate. This should be a central consideration in our tax laws. We should have an industrial policy to cope with this problem. I am told that the Iron Ore Company of Canada will invest some $900,000 for every job it creates. That is a tremendous amount of money to create one job. You can see right there the tremendous incentive we are giving to the extractive and resource industries and the type of economy and unemployment situation that results therefrom.
There are one or two other points of concern that I and my party want to raise in this debate. We are concerned that all income in this country is not treated the same way. If you are a worker in a factory, a nurse or a teacher, you will find that your wages are taxed pretty well to the last dollar. But if you are fortunate enough to possess a large amount of money, it does not matter where you get that money from-it could be from hard work, from investments, from a windfall gain or through inheritance-you are taxed in a different way.
In this country we have only a 50 per cent capital gains tax. We have a dividend tax credit for those who accumulate income from corporations and the clipping of coupons. This difference represents a very dangerous feature in our taxation system. It represents an important value judgment which our country has made about where your money comes from. In essence, we are saying you are more important if your income is derived from the clipping of coupons. This is a very bad principle upon which to start. It is a very discriminating feature in terms of the develop-

ment of our country. In effect, our tax system is based on inequity.
Just a few days ago, when I was speaking in this House on the corporate tax bill, I gave an example of what I meant by different taxes being applied to similar amounts of money. I believe the fundamental principle should again be drawn to the attention of the House. Here I take the example of three single people, male or female, each earning $10,000 per annum. The first person earns that amount of money as a worker in a factory, as a teacher or as a nurse. On that $10,000 he or she is taxed at $2,285 per annum. This person has a friend who earns $10,000 through capital gains. Because we have only a 50 per cent capital gains tax, the friend will pay only $844 tax. A third person also makes $10,000 a year on dividends from corporations, and he will pay only $193 tax.
That is a damning indictment of the type of taxation system we have in Canada, of the type of value judgment we have in this country where we place great value on persons who have a lot of money. We worship these people by giving applying a different taxation system and different rates of taxation. Both in the long run and in the short run, I think that type of system is not good for the country. It is a system that discourages the average worker, the average citizen. Of course, the philosophy of the Department of Finance and of the two old-line political parties is that the person who makes his money through capital gains or dividends will reinvest in the economy, thereby creating jobs and benefiting society as a whole. Mr. Speaker, this is not the most effective way of achieving that end. If you want to stimulate the economy and create jobs, you should be going about it the opposite way; you should be giving a tax break to the small man, putting more money into the pocket of the average citizen. He in turn will purchase more, this in turn will stimulate the economy and encourage more development and more job creation.
I am sure that if the average citizen, the low income person, had enough money to purchase a car, General Motors could still survive and still make a profit. I am sure this is also true of the furniture companies and food processing companies, because then the low income people would have enough money to purchase better quality food and furniture.
That is the philosophy of our party, Mr. Speaker, that we start at the bottom rather than at the top. Nothing can kill the initiative of people who work with their hands and their brains more than to know they are confronted with a tax penalty, to know that they are taxed in a different way from someone who may be fortunate enough to clip coupons or make his income from capital gains. If we could plug those tax loopholes in our taxation system, we would have more productivity; we would the type of economy that would be better for all Canadians, the small businessman, the working man, the farmer.
We need a fair taxation system, a system that uses the tax credit system rather than exemptions. We need a system that will tax all income equally no matter where it comes from, on the theory put forward by the Carter commission that a buck is a buck. We should not differentiate with respect to the type of occupation in which the dollar is earned. We need a full capital gains tax, exclud-
June 18, 1973

ing of course the exceptions that this party has always advocated, the family farm, the homes in which people live, and the small family business. These are some of the steps necessary for our society and economy to prosper. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would much prefer the extractive industries and the resource industries to be taxed in the way that we tax other industries in this country, so that they would bear their fair share of the tax burden.
I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) through you, Mr. Speaker, that we in this party support the bill. I hope the progressive $100 minimum tax cut is a feature that we will see a lot of in the future. This, indeed, could be the beginning of a new taxation system in Canada that would give the average and low income earner a break.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-193 includes numerous amendments to the Income Tax Act. The purpose of the bill is therefore to implement the provisions of the motion concerning income tax of which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) gave notice on May 29, 1973.
One provision of the bill is designed to increase the basic exemption for single persons and married couples.
Mr. Speaker, I will say at the outset that the basic exemption is clearly inadequate, because in my opinion, with the present high cost of living, it would be unfair to levy income tax on individuals who have not even managed to go beyond the poverty line.
The report of the Senate Committee on Poverty says this:
The popular notion that our tax system takes from the rich to give to the poor is a myth.
Mr. Speaker, I know that all the hon. members are convinced of the truth of this statement, because even if we have been working at it for many years, we have not yet succeeded in correcting a situation which is worsening every day.
I keep on quoting:
Fifty six per cent of the income of those earning less than $2,000 (before transfer payments) goes to paying taxes. If social security contributions are included, this becomes 60 per cent of their income. By comparison, those with incomes over $10,000 pay only about 37 per cent in taxes.
And that is still too much, because I know a great number of heads of family with dependents who earn $10,000 a year and yet find it very hard to make both ends meet. Sometimes, they do not manage even if they are thrifty and lead a human, normal and sensible life, without any extravagance.
The committee goes on, and I quote:
Income tax exemption levels must be raised to the level of the appropriate "poverty line" for family units.
This is a problem which has been the subject of special studies by a Senate Committee on Poverty which has attracted the attention of members of the Economic Council of Canada who have very seriously considered this problem and made some recommendations, which this government is very slow in accepting and applying.
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
Among other things, it is strongly recommended as an immediate solution that the income tax be reduced by increasing the basic exemption level in order that taxpayers may have a minimum tax-free income and in order to ensure above all the satisfaction of the needs of individuals and their dependents.
If it is right to believe, on the one hand, that a reduction of the income tax in favour of big corporations will result in increasing the number of jobs in Canada, why on the other hand would a reduction of personal income tax not produce the same results?
If we are justified in hoping, thanks to the previous measure presented to the House, that by granting tax cuts to the large corporations we will stimulate the economy and create jobs, as a result of the increased revenues to these corporations, then I feel that the same results should be obtained by granting income tax cuts to individuals.
If the large corporations benefit from tax cuts, then it is only logical to leave the individual with a greater proportion of his income so that he can have greater purchasing power, in order to obtain more of the items produced by the large corporations.
The corporations might produce more, thanks to an income tax cut. And if we want to be realistic and take things to their logical conclusion, I think that it is our duty as parliamentarians to ensure that the individual's income is also increased, thus enabling him to buy what the large corporations can produce, to encourage increased production and to ensure that economic activity is pursued at full capacity.
In my constituency, a great many factory workers and farmers earn less than $100 a week, or less than $5,000 a year. I know these people. I meet them very often. Last weekend I even met some of them who told me of their problems and their worries.
There is another troubling fact that must be stressed: the Canadian Bill of Rights makes no mention of the economic rights of Canadians. Therefore, I believe there is a gap there. Surely, Canadian citizens have economic rights and the most essential is to be able to have an adequate income allowing individuals, family heads, to discharge their responsibilities in a dignified way, which is possible in 1973 in a country as great and as rich as ours, well provided for in all kinds of natural resources.
The concept of human rights goes back mostly to the Magna Charta, a latin expression which regained currency during consideration of the Bill of Rights. The Magna Charta was granted to England in 1215 by King John. Prior to that, English people were the king's things. There was no fair provision governing the rights of these citizens in order to ensure to all and each of them the equal recognition of their rights.
The Magna Charta sanctioned the political emancipation of the English and proclaimed the following freedoms: personal freedom, inviolability of the individual, alleged innocence till evidence of guilt, inviolability of the domicile, freedom of assembly, freedom of speech and freedom of association.

Income Tax Law (No. 3)
These are therefore important rights. The Magna Charta had a serious deficiency, because it did not refer to the economic rights of the individual and the same thing has been done in Canada. For example, if any individual has the right to live, he is consequently entitled to the necessaries of life. In the past, the family could produce almost everything to satisfy its needs ob could, through barter, obtain goods which it lacked. Then, the workers could expect to produce more than they needed and barter their surplus for other products. Those who, for one reason or another, had no means of living were dependent on social welfare or the co-operative to which they belonged. It was then difficult to do better. Today however, the economy is quite different, the occupations being quite diversified and well classified. Some individuals, for example, will spend their entire lifetime screwing bolts onto automobile chassis; others will do the same casting all year long; that is chain production. Evidently, those people cannot eat or wear bolts or castings, but they exchange the value of their work for wages or money which will enable them to buy what they need.
But if the state, through its income tax laws, deprives them of a certain amount of their money, this keeps them automatically from spending a similar amount on providing for their needs. That is what we are now witnessing. I am not the one who discovered this state of affairs; persons who were paid by the Canadians, through some law or other, to study the problem throughout Canada, did so and suggested means to remedy the situation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, production has become like a giant co-operative to which each producer contributes; the collective production is then offered the Canadian consumers, and each is invited to choose whatever he finds suitable.
Obviously, if I need a tractor I will not buy a horse. So you must choose what you need. It is a free choice. Each individual is entitled to choose what he needs.
This way of producing, mainly with the assistance of science and machinery, is quite effective in achieving a high rate of production and a higher abundance of products for consumers. But then all consumers should be able to enjoy this abundance!
It seems that the time has come in Canada to complete the great Bill of Rights by adding to it a Proclamation of the Economical Rights of the Citizens, which would guarantee to everyone his share of this abundance and I think that even the Minister of Finance fully agrees with me since, when he introduced the motion which preceded Bill C-193, he said that such was the objective. We advocate slightly different ways of achieving it but we have the same objective. To reach this objective we shall eventually have to agree on the way to reach it in the most efficient way possible and to the advantage of the largest possible number of people.
In Canada, everyone is producing; everyone can produce enough goods to meet everyone's needs. Everybody knows that even though Canada is not currently producing enough of those goods, she could do it immediately by simply providing work to thousands of unemployed and by ordering from our industries which at present are operating at half their capacity.

I am convinced of one thing, Mr. Speaker. All hon. members receive each weekend numerous requests of all kinds from young men and young girls or from older people. Their assistance is requested to find a job. These people absolutely want to contribute to the greatness of their country, through their work, to produce something which the Canadian people may need and which are necessary to mankind, and they are available.
Mr. Speaker, I am sometimes angered when I hear people criticize youth saying; young people are lazy, they do not want to work anymore. Such assertions make no sense. I myself know large families with 10, 12, 16, 17 or 18 children, and I have always noted that in these large families, all the children look for a job after completing their studies in order to earn a living.
Last weekend, I met a few graduates from Laval University who asked me if I could help them to find some work. They searched for a job but they cannot find any. They are ready to go to James Bay, in the North in a word, anywhere, to serve their country. I even contacted the minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) to offer him these people's services. This means that young Canadians are available and ready to do something for the development of their country, to produce more in order to meet everybody's needs.
It is therefore our duty, as the elder and responsible people, to do our best to ensure that our laws enable those who still have some initiative to undertake something which might prove successful, in order to create jobs.
I listened this afternoon to the minister of Finance who spoke of 497,000 jobs being created. I believed him. I take his word but that is not enough. Our labour force is growing at a faster rate.
One must go faster than that in order to allow our country to change its method of recording statistics.
Statistics on unemployment are compiled, while statistics on the lack of manpower should also be compiled. An employment insurance act should be passed, instead of an unemployment insurance act-that is the whole difference, Mr. Speaker-in order to be able to work efficiently towards the progress of our country. I would like us to serve our country, to continue its development and to bring more and more Canadians to like their country, to find opportunities enabling them to live in it, and for that purpose very thorough reforms of our financial and monetary systems will have to be brought forth. I am convinced that the hon. Minister of Finance agrees with that. But he is caught in a mesh of circumstances, he must serve a system which refuses to serve in 1973. That is why we want to help him with all our strength. He can rest assured that he will receive our support when he wants to reform our system for financing the public sector.
When we look at statistics and realize that, each morning before the sun rises, we must dig into our pockets and come up, all of us, with $7 million to pay the interests on our public debt, this is preposterous. If we multiply this amount by 365 days, the result is $2 billion. How many things we could do with $2 billion!

Last week, when I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) whether he intended to ask the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) for additional funds so that he might authorize a greater number of projects under the Opportunities for Youth Program, he simply replied: I did not make such a request and have no intention of making any either. Mr. Speaker, this is disappointing for our young people who have submitted worthy projects. We should study these projects drawn up by responsible young people eager to accept, in their country, the invitation of the government which had told them: Prepare projects and submit them to us; then, we shall grant you subsidies which will enable you to do something positive. The budget of the Secretary of State is limited; he can do no more.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), who is now in his place, is aware of many problems with regard to the administration of LIP.
For my part, I feel I have done my duty by making honest and positive suggestions to the minister and the government to help them make a better selection amongst the LIP projects proposed to them, which are prepared, thought out and put down on paper by responsible individuals, but three quarters of which are turned down for lack of money. If it isn't for lack of money, I wonder if it isn't for lack of water; and if that is the case, we should have no problem this year because it rains every day. But that we know: there is no shortage of water, but of money!
With regard to financing the public sector, the Minister of Finance collects income tax by virtue of the Income Tax Act that applies to both individuals and companies, in order to have enough revenue to meet the financial needs of all the departments.
And so, the Minister of Finance is at the very centre of the whole federal administration.
That is why I am confident-and I say this to my country-as I am aware of the sincerity and honesty of the Minister of Finance, that before long he will consider seriously the proposals that have been made to him in order to correct the situation. We should stop financing the public sector of the Canadian administration, and thus bring about a release and enable Canadians to use the savings of individuals. Our private financial institutions could finance more efficiently the private sector and the private sector would become more effective because the money it needs to operate normally would be available.
I believe that Bill C-193 somewhat alleviates personal income taxes. I recognize that and I thank the minister for having done something. But that is not enough. More should be done more quickly so as to change our accounting methods when it comes to our human force, our work force.
Recently I was reading in a magazine published in a European country twice devastated by war, that it is a countdown that it is being done over there. Instead of having statistics on unemployment, they compile statistics on the lack of manpower, and that country, twice devastated, is lending money now to Allied countries, to Canada as well as others. And if there has been a transformation in its financing system, it is because satisfaction
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
was installed in the hearts of those people who served their country well and did their best.
It is distressing to see that young husky and healthy people, whose parents did everything to bring them up decently, have them educated so that they would get the diplomas they needed to earn a living and help their country, are lying sunk in sloth. There is no one to offer them a job when others have not enough time. And yet there are people who, like myself, work 15, 16 or 18 hours a day. We do our utmost to manage the country efficiently using old blunt tools. No matter the worker's ability, if he works with a blunt planer all the wood will be jagged. And yet he has been working very hard.
And this is what is done here. Then, let us manage to change the cylinder while it is still time because as I already read somewhere, our economic system will be reformed by orderly men with us and for us or by disorderly men against us and without us.
We know that nothing but bad can germinate in the mind of those young people who are head over heels in debt. I have been 20 years old once and it would not have been good to let me unoccupied. I worked for 5 cents an hour to sustain myself, but I worked. Nowadays, however, too many people cannot exchange their work for their sustainance.
This situation is difficult to accept in 1973 and Canada cannot afford it and this is why I urge the Minister of Finance to present to the committee, after second reading, amendments improving his bill to make it more generous for the individuals, and the workers to let them enjoy a larger part of the outcome of their work.
If there is anything more needed for administration purposes in the public sector let us get it from the Bank of Canada.
That is just an empty word, it is a meaningless institution.
I remember, Mr. Speaker, that when my leader, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) brought in a measure last winter to amend the Bank of Canada Act, the minister of Finance was in his seat listening attentively; he seemed to say that it would be logical to amend two sections in the Act to enable this institution to grant loans, not for six months, but for 60 years, as is done for certain European or Asian countries.
We may note in passing that even though evil tongues have said that we were against these loans which we grant abroad, that this is completely false. We have said, and 1 say it again, that if loans can be granted to others on such a long-term basis, and at the cost of administering them, why can this not be done in Canada, for the provinces and the municipalities? If the recipe is good abroad, it should also be good in our own country.
Mr. Speaker, the day is not too far off when all Canadians will ask the government, whatever it may be, to do something; its political affiliation is of no importance, what counts is its effectiveness, and more and more Canadians are discovering that a minority government is not such a bad thing for a country, because being in a minority makes the government less deaf, and causes it to

June 18, 1973
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
listen more attentively to the people's suggestions and demands.
We have witnessed this, we have proof of it, and I say that openly. The people whom we meet every weekend say it to us openly: Carry on as you are doing, we want to have a good administration; the government does not matter much, we do not care about that, as long as we are properly administered.
Over the past few months of this 29th Parliament during which we have been sitting, we have passed several good bills which Canada might have missed with a majority government. This means that this assembly of representatives of the nation, Parliament, is the supreme authority. If we assume our responsibilities and pass the best legislation possible, with the intelligence the Creator has endowed us with, we can give our country the best and most up-to-date legislation, while at the same time getting the executive to carry out the wishes of Parliament by administering in an objective and most efficient way possible the acts of Parliament.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, may I assure the Minister of Finance that, if he comes up with amendments likely to improve Bill C-193, even in limited way, we shall do the utmost to facilitate his task, in order that this bill may be adopted as quickly as possible. We are not eager for power or domination, but as Canadians, we make it our ambition to serve as effectively as possible those who are paying us to do so.

Cyril Symes (Sault Ste. Marie): Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-193, to amend the Income Tax Act. I note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is in the House and I would like to welcome him to the city of Sault Ste. Marie; I understand he is travelling there to address some dispirited Liberals.
We must have an equitable tax system; this is necessary for economic and social justice. But an equitable tax system is not in itself sufficient to achieve this goal because if the pattern of government expenditure is unjust, what is to be gained? However, there is no time to go into the question of government expenditure. I should like to deal with this bill in terms of just how equitable it is. There are three major ends accomplished by taxation. It provides goods and services, it seeks to distribute wealth among various groups in the economy, and it stabilizes the economy. It is true the bill before us attempts to redistribute wealth more fairly. It contains provisions to provide for tax credits and to index the tax rate taking into account the cost of living. How does Bill C-193 live up to the principle of equitable taxation? We notice that the personal income tax exemption has been raised. Before, it was $1,000 and it has been raised to $1,500 for a single person and $2,850 for a married couple. But it is important to remember that the $1,000 exemption was based on the cost of living in 1949, and if we are to comply with the principle of fairness we should take into account the cost of living today and apply it to the exemption. If we did so, the personal exemption would not be $1,500, as the government proposes, but at least $1,650 for a single person and $3,280 for a married couple, taking into account the rate of inflation since 1949. The government has at least made a

step but, as is typical of Liberal governments, it has not gone all the way to live up to the idea of fairness.
I think we should take as our guiding principles some of the recommendations of the Carter Commission on Tax Reform. That commission recommended that every citizen should assume his fair share of the total tax burden, that there should be a comprehensive tax base, and that no type of income should be excepted. If we compare this ideal with the realities of today, we find we are confronted with a very serious situation. The Senate report on poverty concluded that those in the lower income groups are still paying more taxes because of our system of hidden taxation. If we look at the figures for 1961 contained in the Senate report, which they are the latest figures available, we find that if a person's income is less than $2,000, taxation amounts to 60 per cent of that income. A person earning between $5,000 and $7,000 pays 32 per cent in tax, and a person making $10,000 and upward pays about 38 per cent of his income in tax.

speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
There are basic injustices in the system, despite talk of reform which the Minister of Finance is so fond of repeating. Moreover, there are built into our tax system some frightening loopholes. I wonder how many people realize that in 1969 the following people paid no income tax whatsoever because of these loopholes: One person made $600,000 and paid not one cent in income tax in 1969. In the income group between $100,000 and $200,000 there were seven people who got away without paying income tax. In the $25,000 to $50,000 range, 98 people were able to escape payment of taxes. Breaking this down into professions, the figures are even more revealing. Two hundred and thirty-four doctors paid no income tax, neither did 128 dentists nor 237 lawyers. So there still remain, in our system, injustices and these must be righted if the government is to be taken seriously on the issue of tax reform.
There are some of the loopholes for individuals, but far greater are the loopholes that exist for corporations. Our party has stressed again and again that we will continue to seek justice for all taxpayers. In 1951, 29 per cent of government revenue was derived from corporations and 27 per cent from individuals. At the end of the fiscal year 1973, it is estimated that corporate income tax as a percentage of government revenue will decline to 16 per cent, whereas individual income tax will account for 43 per cent of government revenue. In other words, over the years corporations have been paying less and less tax and carrying less and less of the tax burden, and individuals have been paying more tax.
In light of this, what is the Minister of Finance proposing to do? He now proposes to reduce corporations taxes even further, from a theoretical percentage rate of 49 per cent to 40 per cent. The Conservatives, of course, support him despite the fact that for the first quarter of this year corporate profits increased by 53 per cent. The NDP say that it is time to give the individual taxpayer a break, and we can do this by making corporations start to pay their fair share. Remember that in 1969, 49 per cent of Canadian
June 18, 1973

corporations avoided paying any federal income tax. In 1973, corporate income taxes are going to decline by some $60 million while personal income taxes will account for $1,125 million additional federal government revenue. Surely there is need for reform in this area.
Another provision of the bill proposes to index income tax so we keep in step with the cost of living. In other words, someone paying 20 per cent of his income in taxes this year will pay the same percentage next year even if inflation increases. This is a good idea so long as the basic tax system is a fair one. If it is not, as I have suggested, then we are merely perpetuating the inequities of the system despite the indexing approach. The poor will still be discriminated against, and the middle income group in this country, not the corporations, will bear the brunt of the burden of taxation.
What we have been proposing over the years is the idea of a tax credit as the best way of overcoming inequities in our taxation system. I am pleased to see that a beginning is being made in the bill in this regard and that the minimum tax credit will be $100, which may rise to $500. This is the fairest way to bring about tax reform in Canada, and it is one of the recommendations of the Carter commission.
The progress that has so far been made in the area of personal income tax is the result of the minority position in which the government now finds itself. Last November, the New Democratic Party produced a shopping list and stated that if the Liberal government wanted our support, one of the top priorities of the government must be a reduction in personal income tax. This the government has done but only, as I have explained, to a certain degree; many inequities in the system still remain. We in our party will not be satisfied until we have a truly fair and equitable system of taxation in Canada, and we shall continue to press for reform in the months and years to come.
I see it is approaching ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, so I shall resume my seat in order that we may proceed with this tax bill.

subtopic: MANPOWER-SUGGESTED COMBINING OF MANPOWER AND UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE OFFICES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
MANPOWER-SUGGESTED COMBINING OF MANPOWER AND UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE OFFICES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 29 last, as reported at page 2729 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) whether he was proposing to introduce legislation to combine Manpower offices and Unemployment Insurance Commission offices. The minister replied that he was examining the relationship between the UIC and Manpower with a view to providing greater co-operation. Later in reply to a supplementary question he said he was examining the whole question in light of current conditions and situations, despite the fact the UIC and Manpower began to operate separately some six or seven years ago.
I am raising this matter in view of a questionnaire that was sent out in my riding. My riding is such that I have to send out at least 57,000 questionnaires to cover all householders, and I have been able to get an 18 to 20 per cent return on those questionnaires. One part of my questionnaire whether Manpower and UIC offices should be combined. Should all federal employment services be under one roof? Should offices be local in each community, and should they have full or at least part-time services? My constituents replied, 90.50 per cent in favour of these changes being made, and 4.29 per cent against.
Another part of the questionnaire asked whether persons qualifying for UIC payments should attend at manpower offices to collect their cheques and get assistance on

June 18, 1973
Adjournment Debate
job applications. Should the computer be dropped and should unemployment counsellors be responsible to issue UIC cheques? To that 75.50 per cent replied yes, while 17 per cent were against.
It has become clear to me as a result of talking with a number of my constituents that by and large Canadians are totally fed up with this mish-mash of Unemployment Insurance offices in one building and UIC offices somewhere else. This House also should be fed up with this situation. We are spending approximately $2 billion per year in unemployment insurance and an additional $500 million this year in Manpower services. We have in this country two agencies separate and distinct, both dealing with the employment situation. One agency is called Manpower and is supposed to look for jobs for people, and the other agency is the Unemployment Insurance Commission which is paying out money to the jobless.
Surely it is time for a rethinking of this situation. It is time this government related jobs to the jobless. We should have a new employment policy rather than an unemployment policy. The philosophy of this government is an unemployment philosophy. We need a new thrust, a new policy; an employment policy. We should relate our search for jobs to the jobless. We must go out and find work for those who want work, and that can only be done by combining these employment agencies under one roof.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission is a remote commission. It concerns itself with sending out forms and computerized cheques. When it discovers on occasion that people are cheating, it sends out its super cops known as benefit-control officers. It is not really concerned one iota with finding work for those who want work. Surely the purpose of an employment agency is to go out into the marketplace and help those who seriously and honestly want work, to find work. The Unemployment Insurance Commission does nothing of the kind; it operates on the philosophy of mailing out cheques, keeping the unemployed happy so they will not bother the commission. In effect, it says, "Don't phone; we will get in touch with you".
Let us consider our Manpower service. It operates with a bunch of schemes. It has a retraining scheme in respect of which it makes payments to those it deems retrainable. Again, it makes those payments without any real reference to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Today we have two arms of the same ministry making payments to people who are unemployed. This is absolutely ridiculous. We have a similar situation in respect of moving allowances. Officers of the Manpower service will suggest to an individual there is not an employment opportunity in one community but there is an opportunity in another, and will pay a moving allowance; yet there is no reference to the Unemployment Insurance Commission in this regard.
We have the problem of temporary work, the situation where there are many jobs in the community that are of a temporary nature. But, unfortunately, if a person on unemployment insurance accepts one of these jobs, in many cases he jeopardizes his claim to unemployment insurance. So we have the unemployment insurance system working against a person legitimately out of work who wants to help himself. A member of the House said

that he cannot get help in the sugar bush. The reason is clear; a job in the sugar bush lasts maybe two or three weeks, and to take that job makes you fully employed. But then you are back in the system and you may have to wait two or three weeks or more to get the unemployment insurance cheque. So we have all sorts of problems of people who could work-

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MANPOWER-SUGGESTED COMBINING OF MANPOWER AND UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE OFFICES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not share the view of the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) that integration of Manpower and Unemployment Insurance offices is essential to achieve effective co-ordination between the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the UIC. The fullest degree of coordination and co-operation is needed to ensure that the unemployed get all the services of both organizations, but that does not necessarily require organizational integration. There is, in fact, a high degree of co-ordination and co-operation at present and interagency committees are actively at work to further strengthen this co-ordination and co-operation.
I might suggest to the hon. member for Peel South that if he wishes to obtain a valid response from his constituents he should put before them the reasons on both sides of the question that he is asking them. I would also suggest that he should put forward, on the side of the argument that he was making, factual claims that are somewhat more accurate. Unfortunately, I do not have time to deal with that this evening.
The reasons for organizational separation of the National Employment Service from the UIC in 1965 and the establishment of the Department of Manpower and Immigration in 1966 are still valid. The reasons were several and I will not go into them in detail here, but I want to mention that the separation was recommended by the committee of inquiry into the Unemployment Insurance Act-the Gill committee-and was supported by the Economic Council of Canada. The basic purposes for that recommendation and for the establishment of the Department of Manpower and Immigration included bringing together the various federal elements concerned with manpower policies and programs in order to develop an integrated approach to the development and implementation of such policies and programs, and to more effectively co-ordinate these with immigration policies and programs.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED RECOMMISSIONING OF CERTAIN DESTROYERS FOR USE IN PROTECTING FISHERMEN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED RECOMMISSIONING OF CERTAIN DESTROYERS FOR USE IN PROTECTING FISHERMEN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid this is going to be another Hansard reporter's nightmare tonight, because I have many things to say and very little time in which to say them. On June 1, 1973, I asked the following question of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson):
-in view of the fact that it would cost about $1.6 million a year to put the four destroyers to sea-we are talking about a total
June 18, 1973

investment in those ships lying alongside amounting to $160 million, so here we are talking about 1 per cent of that investment- and in light of the fact we could probably draw 700 men from the National Defence headquarters and never feel it... will the minister reconsider his decision to let the ships lie alongside and put them back to sea where they could at least assist our fishermen in avoiding the kind of harassment they sometimes experience from larger ships of other nations?
The minister's reply was:
Mr. Speaker, I am certain the hon. member knows that we have recently commissioned three new DDH destroyers which have a much greater capability than the ones to which he is referring.
Put in its most polite form, the answer can only be described as nonsense based upon a massive lack of comprehension of the problem. My impression that the minister's response is based upon misapprehension of Canada's maritime needs is reinforced by the even more fantastic suggestion which he tossed off in response to one of my questions when he appeared before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, that he might sell four destroyers currently lying inactive or, more properly, four of our destroyers so that none would remain inactive.
These replies are so removed from reality that one scarcely knows where to begin to criticize them. First consider the fact that one government department, the Department of the Environment, has caused legislation to be passed in this House extending Canadian fishing limits to 12 miles, based on the straight baseline principle. Further, it has presented legislation asserting Canada's right to exercise control with respect to the potential to pollute over vessels in waters many miles distant from our coast, legislation designed to ensure that our Arctic waters are pollution-free, and now, in co-operation with the Department of External Affairs, is preparing to argue that the International Law of the Sea conference that Canada and other maritime nations should have jurisdiction over fishing and the sea lanes out to the limits of their continental shelves, in Canada's case a distance of approximately 200 miles. That means that the area of the sea, over which Canada legitimately wishes to exert some control with respect to fishing and pollution prevention, might be conservatively estimated at 700,000 to three-quarters of a million square miles.
Second, consider that in order to enforce its wishes out to the limits of the continental shelf, Canada has at its behest the following equipment capable of operating out to 200 miles from the coast or beyond that distance. In the Department of National Defence there are somewhat in excess of 50 aging Argus and Tracker maritime patrol aircraft, both in need of replacement shortly, and any of which, if they observe a violation of our laws, are incapable of effective action to prevent its continuance. The Department of National Defence also has at its disposal three support vessels which are not designed for such tasks, four submarines which can be considered to be only marginally effective in such a role, and 24 destroyers. Of the destroyers, two are not yet in commission, that is, they have not yet left the hands of the builders. I am speaking of the DDH 280 class destroyers. Two others, while in commission, are not expected to achieve operational readiness for another one to one and a half years. All of which
Adjournment Debate
leaves us with 20 destroyers, two or three of which will be under refit at any given time and four of which, I have been informed in answer to order paper questions, at any given time will be incapable of going to sea because they are inadequately manned. Thus, the Department of National Defence at the present time, at any given time, has available for use 13 to 15 vessels capable of enforcing the laws of the land now in effect or contemplated for over three-quarters of a million square miles of ocean.
The Department of Transport has 43 vessels capable of operating as far out as 200 miles from the coast. However, to utilize them in the capacity I am suggesting tonight is necessary would involve abandoning or neglecting such essential services as icebreaking, northern escort service, northern resupply, maintenance of navigational aids such as buoys, weather reporting, and search and rescue. Each of these DOT vessels is already overemployed, so they can be eliminated from our calculations of what is necessary to enforce the laws about which I am speaking this evening.
The RCMP have no vessels capable of operating as far as 200 miles from the coast. The Fisheries Protection Service has five such vessels, four on the east coast and one on the west coast. To exert effective control over the three-quarter million square miles of ocean over which we wish to exert control we would have to have a vessel within 12 hours steaming time of any reported incident. This means approximately 30 vessels ready for sea, or at sea, at any given time. Presently, as I have demonstrated, we may have as many as 19 available for such duties, taking into account all marine services.
Why then, in heaven's name, are we allowing four first-rate destroyers, whose average projected useful life would be ten years and which represent a minimum capital investment of $160 million to $200 million, to lie idle when for a cost of less than 1 per cent per annum of the total capital investment involved, over and above the moneys currently being spent on maintaining them, these vessels could be at sea, being useful? Why are we even considering selling them, when they could be so eminently useful, and their sale would recover only a fraction of their value? Our maritime commanders, east and west, are crying out for more vessels to carry out their assigned tasks, yet at any given time four remain idle for lack of expenditure of an infinitesimal portion of the total defence budget.
For too long DND, largely because of lack of effective political leadership and continuity in political leadership, has been penny wise an pound foolish.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED RECOMMISSIONING OF CERTAIN DESTROYERS FOR USE IN PROTECTING FISHERMEN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I say that it is very seldom we on this side of the House accept a "conservative" estimate from a New Democratic Party member. Leaving out his unrealistic comments regarding National Defence headquarters, the hon. member from Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) will recall that on 1 June when he raised this matter in the House the minister replied:
-we have recently commissioned there new DDH destroyers

June 18, 1973
Adjournment Debate
which have a much greater capability than the ones to which he is referring.
There can be no doubt that a ship equipped with two helicopters will provide a substantially improved capability, in terms of time and space, do carry out surveillance and sovereignty activities when compared to ships that do not have a helicopter capability. The primary responsibility for the regulation and protection of our fishing fleets remains with the Department of the Environment. In addition to this, the Department of Transport operates vessels also employed on regulatory duties.
If anyone in this House is aware of ships, operating costs, the hon. member should certainly be aware that destroyers with their complex design and specialized capabilities are relatively expensive to operate in comparison with patrol vessels. Another factor to be considered is the seasonal nature of the fishery and the relatively short period of the fisheries patrol requirement in relation to a 12-month period. The department is right now providing support to the fisheries protection responsibilities of the Department of the Environment with both Argus and Tracker aircraft. As a result of recent discussions with the Department of the Environment, the Canadian forces aircraft flying hours in support of these operations have been increased from 2,200 hours annually in 1972-73 to 2,440 hours in 1973-74.
In economic terms, therefore, because of (a) relatively high operating costs of destroyers, (b) the seasonal nature of the requirement, and (c) the flexibility provided by aircraft in terms of time and space, it would be uneconomic to employ destroyers on fishery patrol duties.
The basic position is that traditionally Canada has not employed warships for fisheries protection. Warships should only be used as patrol vessels in the event of major encroachments and fisheries patrol vessels are unable to deal with the situation. If it should be decided that circumstances required the presence of warships, we already have sufficient destroyers in operation on both coasts to carry out this role.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-REQUEST THAT COMMISSION MAKE EARLY DECISIONS ON BENEFIT ELIGIBILITY TO AVOID OVERPAYMENT CLAIMS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-REQUEST THAT COMMISSION MAKE EARLY DECISIONS ON BENEFIT ELIGIBILITY TO AVOID OVERPAYMENT CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks are related to a question I asked in the House of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) on May 22, 1973, which appears at page 3596 of Hansard as follows:
In view of the fact that thousands of people who have been receiving and thought they were entitled to unemployment insurance benefits are now being assessed overpayment bills-one of my constituents was recently assessed $2,600 as an overpayment- would the minister instruct that if a person is not entitled to the payments he should be informed sooner than is now the practice in place of the current cruel practice of making payments month after month, leading the recipient to believe he is entitled to the money and then billing the recipient for everything he has received.
I imagine the simple answer from the standpoint of the government is that the recipient should not have applied for unemployment insurance in the first place if he was not entitled to receive benefits. But I would suggest that the way in which unemployment insurance benefits have

been given out in the past tends to lead the general public into believing that they are suckers if, during a period when they are not working for whatever reason, they do not apply.
Benefits have been handed out so loosely that if, for instance, a housewife intends to work during a holiday season for eight weeks, and only eight weeks, her friends are shocked to learn that at the end of her period of employment she has not applied for unemployment insurance. Her friends will point out instance after instance of people on benefit who do not need the money and who do not want a job. Rare would be the resident of Canada who does not know of at least one person who has had or is receiving benefits to which they are not strictly entitled.
The way in which benefits have been passed out has led to demoralization, to a feeling that if everyone else is ripping-off the government, "Why not me", to a feeling that honesty does not pay. The overpayment situation is a reflection of the confusions and misunderstandings associated with unemployment insurance, confusions and misunderstandings shared both by the general public and the administrators. How are the administrators supposed to administrate, and how is the general public supposed to respond when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of the country has said that anyone may apply? The Prime Minister was quoted in the Toronto Star of March 11, 1972, as saying: "You know there are people on unemployment insurance who prefer not to work and they have a perfect right to make that decision ... there should be no stigma attached to that. They paid their unemployment insurance premiums."
Many Canadians have been conditioned to feel that their unemployment insurance payments are like money in the bank, to be drawn out at a high rate of interest at any time the move so strikes them. The government should emphasize that unemployment insurance is just that, insurance against unemployment; just as, for instance, fire insurance is insurance against fire. A person who has insured his house against fire would not consider that all the money he has paid into the policy should be his when he moves out of the house unless, of course, his house has been burned down. Yet thousands of Canadians have been conditioned to feel that somehow they are being cheated unless they get back a bonus from the UIC.
The regulations in the past have been so loosely administered that many people do not in fact know whether or not they are entitled to benefits; so they apply, believing the government will let them know whether or not they are eligible. They will ask questions, and be told that their application will be considered. They will phone, and get different answers from different people. They will write, and receive no answer other than a repetition of a form letter previously sent. Finally, payments arrive. The recipient feels all is well. Months later he gets a visit from an official of the UIC; then, weeks or months later he receives an assessment for an overpayment and often he will owe everything he has received.
The government should bring forward Bill C-175 which is designed to clarify and, when needed, tighten the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We need new legislation to end the confusions and misunderstandings
June 18, 1973

associated with the policies and administration of the unemployment insurance program.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-REQUEST THAT COMMISSION MAKE EARLY DECISIONS ON BENEFIT ELIGIBILITY TO AVOID OVERPAYMENT CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, overpayments arise from different sources, but mainly from lack of information or incorrect information given to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. If the commission is not made aware of the facts for an extended period of time, the overpayment could amount to a substantial amount. Regrettable as the circumstances may be in particular cases, the act is very specific in that benefits incorrectly paid must be repaid to the commission. There is an obligation to repay this money to the Crown regardless of who is in error. I would point out that the commission is always disposed to discuss suitable terms of repayment.
As the hon. member opposite pointed out, there are many confusions and misunderstandings about this program, confusions and misunderstandings which, I might point out, are not helped by his quoting the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) out of context. The hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) at five o'clock this afternoon perpetuated another confusion and misunderstanding when he suggested that those who receive overpayments are asked by the UIC to pay back tax payments
Adjournment Debate
which they have not even received but which have been paid by the UIC directly to the Department of National Revenue. The hon. member is six months out of date, because although that did happen for part of last year the problem has been straightened out this year and no longer occurs.
I might also point out that there are provisions in the unemployment insurance regulations which can be employed to erase an overpayment when it would cause undue financial hardship. I refer to regulation 175, subsection (1), which provides that amounts owing may be declared by the commission to be no longer due and owing in certain cases. Most of these are fairly narrow cases, but the broadest of them is where the commission considers that, having regard to all the circumstances, the sums are uncollectable or the repayment of the sums would result in undue hardship to the claimant. Obviously, the Unemployment Insurance Commission would want to use such discretionary power in very, very limited circumstances. However, the fact is that it does exist in those rare circumstances to which it ought to be applied.
